doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Listening to American radio in Cuba
summary: Short wave radio, antennas and secrecy to hear US stations, seen as the music of the enemy.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Rock music. Why? Even though it was prohibited we went through a lot of different periods where we were even persecuted for playing American music, including rock or jazz. But I always say that Cuba, the Cuban musicians and everybody who loved American music, we have been lucky that the Island of Cuba is just 90 miles away from Key West. So that allowed us to stay informed in many ways, but now we’re talking about music, of what was going on here in the United States. So we were attuned with everything that was going on here in the United States, when the weather permitted. It was not as easy as a lot of people think because in order to listen to the radio stations in the United States you need to have a good short wave radio. You need the second thing was having a good antenna. We had to do a lot of things in order to keep a good antenna on our roof. And the third thing was praying that the weather would be perfect.

You know there’s something about that that lasts and makes an impression I believe on a young person, that you have to go to those lengths to access something like that, and it makes it really special.
Um hum. Say that again? I was talking on my phone.

Okay. When you have to go to those lengths to, you know, get an antenna working and pray for the weather and have a good radio set, it makes that music all the much more special because it’s not easily obtained.

Well it was in my case in particular. I cannot talk about all the other musicians. But in my case in particular, Monk, the struggles that I went through in order to listen to that music, to study that music, so forth and so on, made it very very special. Because it was a long struggle about getting your antenna so forth and so on, and also being careful that your neighbor would not hear it, especially that you were listening to. Because you were listening to a radio station from the United States and at that time unfortunately the political situation in Cuba was that Americans were our enemies. Nowadays, after 52 years still in Cuba they are talking that Americans are going to invade at some point. So I grew up, I went through the missile crisis, I went through Bay of Pigs, I went through all of that, the many attempts by the CIA to overthrow Castro’s government. So it was special. Because listening to a radio station was like promoting the music of the enemy.
Was jazz in particular sort of banned by the Castro regime?
